articles.title: One dead and five missing after explosion destroys building close to Acropolis in Athens
articles.summary: Local media report the property included a holiday rental, with US tourists and a UK national among the missing.

blocks.text: At least one person has died and five more are missing after an explosion destroyed a building in the historic centre of Athens.
The blast happened in the Plaka area of the Greek capital, a neighbourhood close to tourist sites such as the Acropolis, with local media reporting the building housed a holiday rental.
Four American tourists, one British national and a Greek national are said to the people involved - though that has not been confirmed by authorities.
Pictures from the scene showed emergency service workers searching through the rubble, with a gas leak suspected as the cause of the blast.
The body of a woman was found on Saturday morning, with the search ongoing.
The tourists were confirmed to be missing when they did not arrive for their flight at Athens airport, Reuters news agency reported citing local police.
The three-storey building completely collapsed due to the force of the blast, with neighbouring buildings damaged and debris scattered across the road.
Excavators and thermal imaging cameras have been used at the scene to search for survivors.
The explosion happened on a small road situated between two of Athens' most visited sites - the Acropolis and the Temple of Olympian Zeus.
BBC News has contacted the UK Foreign Office.

articles.title: Trump reportedly rejects Iran’s seven-day peace deal to reopen strait of Hormuz
articles.summary:
Tehran awaits official response to plan, but US president is said to expect renewed strikes after midterms

Iran is ⁠awaiting an official US response to its proposal to reopen the strait of…

blocks.text: Iran is ⁠awaiting an official US response to its proposal to reopen the strait of Hormuz and end fighting in the Middle East war as Donald Trump was reported to have rejected the deal.

Iran raised the diplomatic initiative at the UN general assembly in New York, saying it had been transmitted ⁠to the Americans via Qatari mediators and could ⁠reopen the strategic waterway and put an end ​to hostilities in the region within seven days.

But the US president is sceptical and has told his staff that he sees a renewed bombing campaign as likely after the November US midterm elections, the Wall Street Journal reported, citing unnamed US officials.
Earlier, a US official had ⁠said discussions with Iran through mediators were “positive and constructive”.

Iran has offered to reopen the strait of Hormuz and resume talks on its nuclear programme in seven days if the US lifted its naval blockade of Iranian ports, waived sanctions on Iranian oil sales and observed a ceasefire that would include Lebanon.

The Iranian foreign minister, Abbas Araghchi, detailed the proposal to reporters outside the UN security council on Friday, saying the country would also restart stalled talks with the US on Iran’s nuclear programme. “The seven-day timeline will start as soon as the United States accepts this plan,” he said.

Araghchi said the initial steps would take about four to five days to complete, and the strait would be open on the sixth day. “And on day seven, the talks with the US will be started for the final deal on mutually agreed subjects,” he said, referring to the nuclear programme.
“If there is seriousness on the US side to ⁠come to a deal and reopen the strait of Hormuz, everything is now prepared,” Araqchi said.

The Iranians also engaged their Saudi rivals regarding the strait, underscoring the stakes of a seven-month-old conflict that has disrupted oil flows through one of the world’s most critical shipping lanes and taken a toll on the global economy.

Iran’s president, Masoud Pezeshkian, in an interview with the CBS show Face the Nation, said Tehran was ready for talks on its nuclear programme and other issues, but would not accept “bullying or coercion”.
“Iran is not seeking war, but will defend itself against pressure, threats and attacks,” Pezeshkian said, adding that it had already agreed that “we’re not supposed to develop nuclear weapons“.
Previous attempts at diplomacy have failed ‌to end the war, which began on 28 February with US and Israeli attacks.

blocks.caption: Donald Trump during his address to the UN general assembly. Photograph: Mike Segar/Reuters

blocks.text: Since then the war has alternated between pauses and renewed strikes, killing thousands while degrading Iran’s conventional forces and damaging its already ailing economy.

Trump has previously said he was in no rush to reach a deal, even as high oil prices fuel inflation. On the Iranian side, there are questions as to whether the hardliners who dominate the security forces would accept compromises championed by moderates such as Pezeshkian.

Diplomatic efforts surrounding the UN general assembly underscored the global stakes in the conflict, which has disrupted oil flows through one of the world’s most critical shipping lanes and drawn in regional and world powers.
Early on Saturday, Yemen’s ⁠Saudi-led ⁠coalition said ⁠it ​intercepted ‌two ‌drones ‌launched by the Iran-backed ‌Houthis towards ​the ⁠Saudi ​capital, Riyadh.

Iranian-aligned militias in Iraq have been blamed for a pipeline attack that temporarily took more Saudi oil off the market. All the while, Iranian-backed Hezbollah has been engaged with Israeli forces in Lebanon.
With Reuters and AP

September 26, 2026
Dobrindt seeks 'hardening' of EU borders at Munich talks
Several European Union interior ministers are meeting in Munich this afternoon to discuss tightening the bloc's migration policy.
A spokesperson for German Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt told the Münchner Merkur newspaper that the talks will focus on the "implementation of a shift in migration policy."

The 17 ministers will discuss "further refining the European Migration Pact, consistently hardening the European Union's external borders, and accelerating returns from Europe," the spokesperson added.
Germany and Denmark, Austria, the Netherlands, and Greece are due to hold separate talks about the creation of deportation centers or return hubs in third countries.
Germany hopes to secure a deal with a country in Africa or possibly Asia by the end of the year.
Dobrindt's spokesperson said the EU's border agency, Frontex, could be turned into a "border protection and genuine return agency."
Currently, EU member states are responsible for returning asylum seekers whose applications have failed.
EU Commissioner for Internal Affairs and Migration Magnus Brunner will also attend the Munich talks.

articles.title: Whistleblower alleges millions of Driscoll’s berries sent to Canada with excess chemical levels
articles.summary: A whistleblower lawsuit in California is alleging millions of pounds of Driscoll's fruit containing non-compliant levels of pesticides and chemicals crossed the border into Canada, and the company…

image.caption: A pack of Driscoll’s raspberries sold in Montreal. A whistleblower lawsuit is alleging millions of pounds of the company's fruit containing non-compliant levels of pesticides and chemicals crossed the border into Canada, and the company tried to cover it up. (Gloria Henríquez/CBC News)

blocks.text: Montreal·New

A whistleblower lawsuit in California is alleging millions of pounds of Driscoll's fruit containing non-compliant levels of pesticides and chemicals crossed the border into Canada, and the company tried to cover it up.
Lawsuit claims about 50% of shipments from 2022-24 had fruit exceeding Canadian safety levels
Driscoll’s berries are on many Canadians’ plates and all over Canadian grocery stores, with their tagline claiming to be “only the finest berries.”

But a whistleblower lawsuit in California alleges the finest berries were not sent to Canada: instead, millions of pounds of fruit containing non-compliant levels of pesticides and chemicals crossed the border, and the company tried to cover it up.

California resident and former Driscoll’s employee David Harada claims in the lawsuit that by Driscoll’s own estimates, about 50 per cent of all shipments to Canada from 2022 to 2024 had fruit that exceeded Canadian safety levels.
“And it's something where you start seeing it so regularly and you know that something's not right that you have to speak up,” Harada said in an interview with CBC News.

Harada was Driscoll’s manager of food safety and regulatory compliance for the U.S. and Canada. He filed a lawsuit for unlawful retaliation against Driscoll’s. In the lawsuit’s filing, Harada said he felt that he was being set up to be the “scapegoat” for compliance issues and that he was being retaliated against for speaking up.

Harada told CBC he first started noticing problems regarding pesticide safety and over-application in 2022 and reported them immediately to his bosses. He says he brought his concerns to upper management but was told it was something he’d have to manage.
“I had a conversation with my director as to whether or not they had plausible deniability regarding this issue,” Harada said.
CFIA inspected Driscoll’s berries sold across Canada

The Canadian Food Inspection Agency (CFIA) confirmed to CBC News it conducted several inspections on Driscoll’s berries sold in grocery stores across the country between 2022-24 and found chemical levels above the legal limit in Canada.
The chemicals include bifenthrin, iprodione and captan: fungicides and insecticides.
However, the CFIA says the inspections did not lead to recalls, or a corrective action was implemented and the investigations were closed.

items: Independent scientist resigns from pesticide regulator over transparency concerns

blocks.text: Some investigations were also triggered after reports of suspected illness after eating Driscoll's blueberries, or by complaints of chemical taste and smell. The CFIA said the reported illness could not be definitively linked to the berries.

“The cases you have identified involve different products, pesticide residues, importers and locations over a period of several years,” the CFIA wrote in an email to CBC News. “The presence of the Driscoll’s brand on the products does not, on its own, establish that the non-compliances originated from a single producer or source.”
The CFIA says it takes appropriate action depending on the magnitude of the health risk.
Whistleblower alleges Driscoll’s sent millions of berries with excess chemical levels to Canada
Actions include notifying the producer or importer, the specific supplier and follow-up inspections.
Recalls are issued if Health Canada determines that a product poses an unacceptable health risk.
What are the health risks from tainted berries?
Stéphane Bayen, an associate professor in the department of food science and agricultural chemistry at McGill University says berries are often found to have chemical residues above the legal limit.
“That's not something abnormal completely, but definitely that's not what we would like to see and we want to reduce this,” Bayen said.

“Exceedance one time of the maximum residue limit might not be translated as a risk for the health of consumers. That’s where the discussion needs to happen and to make sure that this is not becoming a regular thing.”
Toxicologist Daniel Green says the levels of chemicals found in the CFIA-tested berries wouldn’t make someone sick from eating just a few.
“To get an effect, one would have to eat 19 kilograms,” Green said from one example.
Green says the problem is the exposure to all other toxins combined over time: from food and the environment.
“It is the chemical lifetime exposure experience that has to be looked at,” Green said.

items: Fresh strawberries were a summer luxury. When did they become an all-season toddler snack?
Carney government passes law allowing authorization of banned pesticides

blocks.text: That’s what worries Harada and motivated him to speak out.
He believes the potentially tainted berries crossed the border because in 2022, Driscoll’s removed the food safety and compliance tracking system it had for Canada in order to sell more here.

Harada says that the system ensures there is enough time between the last application of pesticides on the fruit and when it's picked — which allows enough time for chemicals to break down, preventing residues from being over the legal limit.

He accused Driscoll's of wilfully concealing information about the berries’ toxicity levels and told them in order to fix all the issues, the company needed to go public about the violations and potential harms and issue recalls.
“I completely believe that I was part of a coverup because they chose not to disclose this information publicly,” Harada told CBC News.
Driscoll’s says it ‘responded correctly’
Even though Harada says the company asked him to reinstate the tracking system, they didn’t go public and he says he was pushed to resign.

In an email to CBC, Driscoll’s says it cannot comment on the details of Harada’s employment due to confidentiality issues. But it said it “remains confident that the complete factual record will demonstrate that it responded correctly to the concerns Mr. Harada raised, at all times acted in good faith, and at all times conducted itself appropriately."
It also denies removing the food safety tracking system and other allegations in Harada’s lawsuit, adding the company has never knowingly shipped products it believed to be unsafe.

“There will be an appropriate time in the litigation for Driscoll’s to present its own evidence, which we believe will show a very different picture from the one Mr. Harada has presented publicly,” Driscoll’s statement read in part.
Harada says it has not been easy living with the stigma of being a whistleblower, but he thinks it was the right call.
“Canada as a whole deserves more and consumers of any products deserve to feel safe when consuming it,” he said.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Gloria has been a journalist in Montreal for more than a decade. Prior to joining CBC, she reported in three languages and five different countries for Global News, France 24, Berliner Zeitung and Diario La Tribuna in her native Honduras.

articles.title: Jacob Tremblay can relate to the Unabomber. No, really
articles.summary: Canadian actor Jacob Tremblay talks about his new film, Unabomber, and the struggle to empathize with a killer.

image.caption: Jacob Tremblay appears as Ted Kaczynski in Unabomber. The Netflix film focuses mostly on the mail bomber's early life as a student at Harvard. (Philippe Bosse/Netflix)

blocks.text: It's uncomfortable to make any comparison — especially to the actor's face — between Ted Kaczynski, the mass-murdering ecoterrorist widely known as the Unabomber, and Jacob Tremblay, the cherubic former child actor behind films with titles as fuzzy and feel-good as Good Boys and Wonder.
There is some additional context here: After all, we are talking about the 19-year-old Canadian's portrayal of Kaczynski in the Unabomber Netflix movie, which dropped Friday.
But it still feels genuinely offensive to imply that there's any weightier parallel between the two. Which is why it's so surprising when Tremblay himself offers something like it, all on his own.

"I really had a hard time relating to Ted for the most part. But once I was there on set — the script is written so beautifully, of course you can really feel empathetic towards this guy," he says during a video call promoting the film.
Canadian actor Jacob Tremblay embraces his dark side in new film
It is a somewhat striking idea. Even as he points to the terrible, inexcusable crimes Kaczynski committed later, Tremblay keeps returning to his inability to resist relating to him.
"What I found, and what I really held on to," he says, "was the idea of being the youngest person in the room."

He's referring to the stranger-than-fiction beginning to Kaczynski's story — the near-singular plot focus of the Janus Metz-directed film. A math prodigy, the Chicago native was propelled to academic heights at Harvard University at just 16.

Through that early enrolment, he eventually became, at the time, the youngest-ever assistant professor at University of California, Berkeley (at which he would twice plant bombs, some 20 years later).
"You know, in this industry, I'm also often the youngest person there," Tremblay says. "So I could kind of relate to that feeling of awkwardness and not really fitting in."
Bigger backstory
The subject matter, of course, runs deeper than that. At Harvard, Kaczynski was also wrapped up in one of the most bizarre historical confluences of the last century.

After he was selected as a vulnerable test subject for what many have theorized was part of the CIA's top-secret MK-Ultra mind-control experiment, psychologist Henry Murray encouraged the young math student's nascent theories and developed his delicately blooming self-confidence.

He then had him strapped to a chair, wired with electrodes, and saw those same ideas mocked with surgical precision. The subjects were given, in Murray's words, "vehement, sweeping, and personally abusive" critiques that systematically tore them down.

In the movie, the goal is to win the Cold War. If America can figure out how to break young men's minds, they can theoretically then break the minds of captured enemy combatants. And if the goal is to learn how to destroy a person's self-worth, who easier to start with than a precocious, self-unassured child?

The resultant screaming and scheming villainy we get onscreen is an against-type performance for Tremblay, in what he calls a fun change. His filmography, he says, is built around his desire to never play the same character twice, while flitting between as many genres as possible.

But it's this one that has that personal parallel to return to. Because if you're to believe some sources, that was Kaczynski's rosebud, though he had long denied those sessions affected him much at all. Going by the film, they were a gross betrayal of the societal duty to protect children — producing a man who would go on to mail deadly letter-bombs to authority figures for decades.

items: Robert Pattinson's Primetime hates Chris Hansen
Clement Virgo says Steal Away is his most ambitious work yet

blocks.text: Given that this role comes so soon after Tremblay's performance as a boy manipulated into armed resistance against the federal government in Sovereign, the pattern is hard to ignore. The theme of "a young, impressionable mind, driven by trauma, really, to do violent things," as Tremblay characterizes it, that he also deems Unabomber's key message.

"How important it is to treat children with love … and teach them how much value they have," he says. "Because on the flip side of that, if a child isn't loved as much, it's harmful and it causes violence. It really does."

It also comes as the industry in which he came up goes through another period of reckoning. Following former child actor Hayden Panettiere's overdose death earlier this year, Canadian actor Alison Pill wrote a New York Times op-ed calling child acting "extractive, exploitative and nonconsensual" while proposing it should be banned entirely.

Nicky, Ricky, Dicky & Dawn's Casey Simpson, among others, pushed back against a ban — but said propelling a child to stardom basically guarantees they will later feel like a failure, regardless of what they achieve as an adult.
Canadian actor Jacob Tremblay discusses his passion for filmmaking

Tremblay does not make this comparison so directly. And from his earliest memories, his relationship with acting was obsessive fascination: After his first film role in Smurfs 2 at five years old, he says he remembers his mother asking him if this is what he would like to keep doing. Not only did he say yes — he said he couldn't picture ever doing anything else.

That has stayed. After Tremblay briefly flirted with the idea of going to film school, director Mike Flanagan advised him to simply spend as much time as possible on set to prepare for his growing yearning to write and direct.
Even still, as clear as the path to acting may have been, the question of whether he consciously chose it is tougher to answer.

"It's hard to say, 'OK, well, I really wanted to do this when I was five years old,'" he says. "Because I'm sure I couldn't fully understand what it meant to be an actor, or in film, at five years old."

items: Jacob Tremblay on child stardom, The Little Mermaid and Justin Bieber
Child actor Jacob Tremblay hopes Hollywood bites on his zombie script

blocks.text: That leads to the difficult comparison: Kaczynski, the young man raised to an incredibly high level while still too young to handle it, is destroyed. Is that in any way similar to Tremblay's experiences — breaking into fame with his role in the film Room at just eight years old — even if he didn't know what he was signing up for?
"You try and find those parallels, for sure. And I can imagine how different my life would be without this career. It's hard to even think about, right?
"It makes me really feel for someone who — like Ted, who has so much talent at a young age and had so much potential," he says.

"I just really hope that people watching this movie can think about this going forward — about talented people, people with skills. And how they want to elevate them and bring them up in life, rather than using them."

articles.title: Mothers crossing the Mexico-U.S. border risk everything to reunite with their children
articles.summary: While the migrant caravans may have disappeared from Tijuana, and this Mexican border city is no longer the waiting room for entry into the U.S., there are still those seeking to cross. Many who risk…

image.caption: Dina Ramos, seen at the Madre Asunta shelter in Tijuana, Mexico, on Sept. 16, was caught days earlier trying to cross the Mexican border to get back to her six children who were all born in the U.S. (Alessandro Molatore/CBC)

blocks.text: Maria says the smugglers formed a human ladder and told her to climb up by grabbing their shoulders and the steel bars of the border wall between Mexico and California.

The human smugglers picked a spot along the border wall near Tecate, a municipality about 50 kilometres east of Tijuana. It was June, and Maria was trying to return to the U.S. to be reunited with her twin sons and husband in California. She was with a group of about five others also trying to cross.
Maria says a young man was the first to scale up the human ladder and over the border wall. She was told to go up next and started to climb.

"Then I heard and saw that [U.S. Border Patrol] trucks started to arrive," said Maria, in an interview earlier this month with CBC News at the Instituto Madre Asunta shelter for women and children in Tijuana.
Mexican moms willing to risk it all to see their kids in the U.S.
Maria says she fell back on the Mexican side and landed among shrubs with thorns and the group started running. She says she doesn't know what happened to the young man who made it over the wall.
CBC News is not using Maria’s full name because she fears repercussions for her attempts to enter the U.S. twice in the past 10 months.
While migrant caravans from Tijuana have disappeared and this Mexican border city of about 2.3 million is no longer the waiting room for entry into the U.S., there are still people seeking to cross.

Many who risk the journey have been separated from their families by deportation, including mothers who are trying to get back to their children, advocates say. And they're choosing more dangerous, clandestine routes that cost tens of thousands of dollars with narrow margins of success.
She says she fell back on the Mexican side and landed among shrubs with thorns and the group started running. She doesn’t know what happened to the young man who had made it over the wall.
Maria says her husband, who is still in California, arranged for her failed attempt to cross the border in June, but she doesn't know how much he paid. "The only thing I know is that we owe money."

items: Mexican woman fighting deportation in Montreal fears for autistic son
Canada’s Mexico visa requirements limit country’s tourism potential, says tour operator

blocks.text: Vitalina Pietrobiassi, the director of the shelter run by the Catholic order of Scalabrinian Missionaries, says the Mexico-U.S. border is a place of "pain" and "separation" for many.
"The women who are deported come here to find a way out of their desperation," said Pietrobiassi.
Smugglers charge up to $25,000 US

Next door, Raul Ochoa is the executive director at House of the Migrant, a shelter for men also run by the Scalabrinians. He says that based on conversations he's had, human smugglers in the area are now charging between $15,000 to $25,000 US to move people across the border.

The low end of the smuggling price spectrum may mean following a guide to a remote spot where surveillance is weak, Ochoa says, adding that paying top dollar could get you guaranteed passage through a port of entry under an arrangement with a U.S. Customs and Border Protection agent.
Crossing into the U.S. right now has a low probability of success, he says, even if one has the money to pay human smugglers known as coyotes.
"The border is basically sealed, there is a lot of security, and the price to pay a coyote is extremely high."

Dina Ramos is also staying at the Instituto Madre Asunta. Ramos, a mother of six children who were all born in the U.S. where she lived undocumented for more than 20 years, says she was caught by U.S. authorities on Sept. 13, while trying to slip across the border.
Ramos would not share details of her crossing attempt, but says she was trying to get back to her family in the U.S. after she returned to Mexico in July to see her ailing parents.
"My children are over there, on the other side, and that's what hurts," she said.

items: Migrants and advocates call on Ottawa for permanent status, with 11 rallies across the country

blocks.text: Ramos says she's desperate to be with her children and plans to find another way across the border.
"One does many things for love," she said.
"I am going to ask for direction from God. I have faith in Him and He is the only one that can help me."
Applying to come to Canada

Ramos was one of more than 10,000 people intercepted since last October by U.S. border authorities in the San Diego Sector. The sector covers roughly 96 km of land border from the Pacific Ocean west of Tijuana to the Tecate region.
This figure is a sharp drop from the approximately 320,000 apprehensions recorded in that area between October 2023 and September 2024, according to U.S. border data.

U.S. Department of Homeland Security and U.S. Customs and Border Protection issued a statement on Sept. 16 saying that apprehensions along the U.S.-Mexico border had dropped by more than 90 per cent since December 2023.

Tijuana immigration lawyer Soraya Vazquez, deputy director of Al Otro Lado, an organization that provides legal and humanitarian support to migrants and refugees, says many of the people still willing to risk crossing the border are deportees trying to get back to their families.
"It's something that is still happening, most of all, yes, with deported mothers who left their families, their children," said Vazquez. "They will always have a yearning to return."
For Maria, staying in Tijuana is not an option. She says she wants to get back to her twin sons — one is set to join the U.S. Marines — and her husband.

Maria, originally from the state of Mexico, has lived undocumented in the U.S. for years. She says she has managed to cross irregularly between the two countries twice. In December 2024 she received word that her oldest son had suffered a massive heart attack at age 29, and she rushed back to Mexico. He died before she arrived and she stayed for a year after.

items: U.S. deporting thousands of Mexican migrants to Central American countries

blocks.text: She says the family considered moving to Canada because her U.S.-born twins would have no issues entering the country.

Maria hired an immigration lawyer in Mexico City who she says got her an appointment with the Canadian embassy in the fall of 2025. At that appointment, she says, a Canadian official took her photo, fingerprints and interviewed her.
"The person who interviewed me told me, 'Good luck,' and that he believed I was a good person," Maria said.

But she says Canadian officials rejected her application and she was never told why. So, in December 2025, she decided to put her life in the hands of human smugglers and cross into the U.S. through the Mexican border state of Sonora, which borders Arizona.
'The dream ends here'

Maria says she was with a group of about half a dozen people who walked for three days through the desert and mountainous borderlands. On the third day, at about 2 or 3 a.m., they believed they had successfully managed to make it across.
"And then all these flashlights turned on," she said.
"It was immigration and they told us, 'Stop walking, don't advance, stand there.' They had dogs."
On the ground at the border wall between the U.S. and Mexico

Maria says she'd been travelling with another mother and her 14-year-old son. She says the mother told her she was trying to save the boy who no longer wanted to go school and was getting involved with people linked to crime.
"She cried. All that effort, all those bruises, all those falls, it stays here, the dream ends here," said Maria.

They were all handcuffed and made to walk what Maria says felt like a long distance to a bus that took them to the Central Arizona Florence Correctional Center about 100 km southeast of Phoenix, Ariz.

items: In the Arizona desert, a race to help migrants who have just crossed the border

blocks.text: Maria was assigned a lawyer who recommended she plead guilty at her court hearing before a judge in Tucson, Ariz. After her plea, Maria was deported back to Mexico about a week before Christmas. She'd spent about two weeks incarcerated.
Despite her two failed attempts, Maria says she plans to try again to get to her sons.
"It's tough. At first, it's a nightmare, but that nightmare can turn into a dream," she said.
"A dream I want to reach in the future … to be with my family, to be united."

articles.title: What Canada's wastewater reveals about drug use in 8 cities
articles.summary: New StatCan data shows sharply different drug-use patterns across eight Canadian cities, with methamphetamine elevated in parts of the Prairies and Moncton, cocaine comparatively high in Halifax and…

image.caption: A woman smokes drugs from a pipe on Dundas Street in downtown London, Ont., in August 2026. The latest StatCan figures offer a window into which drugs are showing up most prominently in different communities. (Alessio Donnini/CBC)

blocks.text: Canada·New

New StatCan data shows sharply different drug-use patterns across eight Canadian cities, with methamphetamine elevated in parts of the Prairies and Moncton, cocaine comparatively high in Halifax and fentanyl highest in Metro Vancouver.
New StatCan data shows starkly different drug-use patterns across 8 Canadian cities
Flush a toilet in Prince Albert, Sask., and the wastewater tells a very different drug story than it does in Halifax or Vancouver.
New Statistics Canada data shows striking differences in drugs detected in wastewater across eight Canadian cities:

items: Methamphetamine and cocaine levels were highest in Prince Albert and also elevated in Saskatoon and Moncton, N.B.
Halifax had the lowest methamphetamine levels but comparatively high cocaine levels.
Fentanyl remained dramatically higher in Metro Vancouver than elsewhere.

blocks.text: The StatCan survey measures drug metabolites — chemical byproducts excreted after the body breaks down drugs — in wastewater samples collected during one-week sampling windows every two months.
The data, from January 2024 to March 2026, covers catchments serving about 9.2 million people. StatCan cautions that it doesn't show exactly how many people use a drug or how much they consume.
But it is a "pretty good proxy of drug consumption" within the area served by a treatment plant, StatCan analyst Sianne Kuang told CBC News.
Prince Albert
Prince Albert had the highest methamphetamine levels of any city monitored and the greatest fluctuations in both methamphetamine and cocaine.
In March 2026, its estimated methamphetamine load was 2,003 milligrams per 1,000 people per day — more than nine times Toronto's roughly 214 milligrams.

"There's many different drivers of different substance use, and one of them is just what is available in the market," said Kora DeBeck, a professor in the School of Public Policy at Simon Fraser University.
Saskatoon
Saskatoon also recorded some of the highest methamphetamine levels, along with Moncton, but behind Prince Albert. Its March 2026 reading was about 958 milligrams per 1,000 people per day.
DeBeck said regional patterns may be connected to how drugs reach local markets.
"It seems much more connected to drug trafficking and how the networks of drug production and trafficking work, and we really don't have good insight into that."
Edmonton
Edmonton's methamphetamine load reached about 1,071 milligrams per 1,000 people per day in January 2025 and stood at 624 in March 2026 — nearly three times Toronto's level that month.
Moncton
Moncton also recorded some of the highest methamphetamine levels.
Methamphetamine was involved in 63 per cent of stimulant toxicity deaths in New Brunswick in 2024 — the highest share involving methamphetamine among Atlantic provinces, StatCan noted.
Moncton joined the survey in March 2025, providing less data from which to identify trends.
Halifax

In March 2026, it recorded just 56 milligrams of methamphetamine per 1,000 people per day, the lowest among the cities monitored, while cocaine was about 1,734 milligrams. Prince Albert's cocaine reading was about 5,296 milligrams — roughly three times Halifax's.

Cocaine was involved in 86 per cent of stimulant-related deaths in Nova Scotia in 2024, compared with 14 per cent involving methamphetamine. Earlier CBC reporting also documented cocaine's growing role in drug-related deaths in the province.
Monty Ghosh, an addiction physician and researcher at the University of Alberta, said local production, using different precursors, formulas and mixtures, can create distinct regional supplies.
"They don't have the same formula they're using. They don't use necessarily the same compounds or drugs."
Metro Vancouver
Metro Vancouver consistently recorded the highest fentanyl levels of all eight cities.
Average levels declined in 2025 and early 2026 compared with 2024, a change StatCan says coincided with a drop in Vancouver's unregulated drug death rate.
DeBeck cautioned against viewing fentanyl's prevalence simply as a response to demand.
"People didn't demand or want fentanyl in the beginning. It just arrived and was there, and then people became dependent on it," she said.

Ghosh said falling fentanyl measurements don't necessarily capture everything happening in the opioid supply, noting that "there's different forms of fentanyl out there, which may not be measured here."
Toronto
Toronto's methamphetamine levels were far below those recorded in Prince Albert and Saskatoon, but another stimulant stood out.
Across available reporting months from July 2024 to March 2026, Toronto had the highest average MDMA levels of the eight cities, at about 40 milligrams per 1,000 people per day.
Montreal
Montreal stood out for comparatively low levels of several opioids measured in the study.
Its codeine levels were the lowest among the participating cities, never exceeding about 44 milligrams per 1,000 people per day, compared with a combined-city average ranging from about 97 to 219.
Montreal also recorded the lowest methadone levels and some of the lowest oxycodone and morphine readings.
Its stimulant profile was closer to Toronto's, with relatively low methamphetamine and comparatively higher MDMA readings.
Wastewater can help illuminate patterns, Ghosh said, but it shouldn't be read in isolation.
"It's only one part of the picture."
Commuting, tourism and temporary population changes caused by special events can introduce uncertainty into the estimates, StatCan cautions.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Eric Michael Johnson is a senior writer and editor based in Vancouver. Before joining CBC, he was an award-winning science writer and editor. He holds a PhD in the history of science from the University of British Columbia. He can be reached at eric.johnson@cbc.ca.

articles.title: Lula bans fixed-odds sports betting a week before Brazilian elections
articles.summary:
President’s ‘hard, drastic and necessary measure’, likely to attract widespread public support, polls suggest

Brazilian president, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, has signed an order banning…

blocks.text: Brazilian president, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, has signed an order banning fixed-odds sports betting just over a week before the first round of the presidential election, in a move he said was designed to tackle the pervasive problem of families falling into debt.
The decision ends the operation, offering, intermediation and advertising of betting.

The provisional executive order comes into force immediately but will need congressional approval within 120 days to remain in effect. It prohibits new deposits into accounts and gives users of betting platforms until 5 October to withdraw their funds.

Lula’s government has also drafted a bill to establish criminal offences related to fixed-odds betting – the most common and dominant type of online sports betting – such as promoting them and using personal data to solicit punters.
“I made the decision to take a hard, drastic and necessary measure,” he told journalists in São Paulo. “It’s like cancer, you take out the tumour, or the tumour will kill us.”
Lula had also criticised the betting industry earlier this week at the United Nations general assembly, accusing it of “transforming addiction into profit” and of “destroying homes”.
Polls suggest a ban enjoys widespread support among Brazilians. Flávio Bolsonaro, Lula’s main rival in the upcoming election, accused the current leader of an “electoral measure”.

Brazil’s president has sharply criticised online betting at least since April, when he called for a ban. The public backlash against it grew during the Fifa World Cup when advertisements were ubiquitous and the number of people betting surged.

Betting and gambling are estimated to cost Brazilian society 38.8bn reais (£5.6bn) annually and increases suicide and depression, according to a 2025 study by the nonprofit Institute of Studies for Health Policies.

The country’s central bank estimated last year that Brazilians spend about 30bn reais on bets each month. That figure included spending by beneficiaries of the cash-transfer federal welfare programme Bolsa Familia (family grant), which was blocked from those platforms last year.
Lawmakers, including many from Flávio Bolsonaro’s Liberal party, struck down a Lula order for tax hikes on online betting and virtual casinos in October last year.

Gambling is illegal in Brazil, but the country opened the gates to online betting in 2018 during the presidency of Michel Temer. The phenomenon snowballed under the watch of the former president, Jair Bolsonaro, Flávio Bolsonaro’s father.

In December 2023, Lula signed a law to regulate and tax betting companies for the first time. Months later, his administration blocked more than 2,000 online betting websites that were designated as irregular, including some linked to criminal organisations such as the First Capital Command from São Paulo and the Red Command of Rio de Janeiro. It was part of a national push to regulate the sector.

Lula and members of his administration have spoken about banning online betting as necessary to both close a drain to the country’s economy and to tackle a public health issue, as many Brazilians are addicted and in financial difficulties due to spending their money on these platforms.
Business analysts say that revenues for sports betting, one of the betting models banned on Friday, are estimated at more than $4bn (£3bn) per year in Brazil, one of the biggest markets in the world.
Before Friday’s move, Brazil’s main football clubs sounded the alarm after betting companies reportedly warned that their sponsorships would end immediately if the government banned betting.
They said the move could lead to the end of Brazilian football, a claim mocked by some social media users in the football-mad country.

articles.title: Bangkok roads submerged as flood disaster declared
articles.summary: An emergency has been declared across the capital of Thailand as days of heavy rain leave the city inundated.

blocks.text: Disaster declared as heavy rain sparks Bangkok flooding
A flood emergency disaster has been declared across Bangkok after 48 hours of heavy rain left roads in the Thai capital submerged.
People have been urged to stay at home and those living close to the city's network of canals have been advised to move their belongings to upper floors.

Thunderstorms are common in Thailand at this time of year but extreme weather in recent days has inundated Bangkok's drainage system, causing traffic chaos on roads that are already famously congested.
The rain is expected to continue into Sunday, raising fears that more canals could burst their banks.
Image source, Getty Images
Canals across the Thai capital have burst their banks, leaving roads under water
Somkid Pheuk-ngam, a 67-year-old who lives near a canal just north of central Bangkok, told the AFP news agency: "The water keeps coming in. It's hard to go out now. It's like at my waist level now.
"I cannot go anywhere. I have been closing my shop for two days now."
She said water levels in the city appeared to be worse than in 2011, when Bangkok was impacted by nationwide flooding.
Hundreds were killed across Thailand then in an extreme weather event that lasted for three months. So far, no casualties have been reported in Bangkok from this latest flooding.
The Thai Meteorological Service has forecast more heavy rain through the week, though the area of low pressure causing the downpours of recent days is expected to move towards central Thailand.

blocks.caption: People holding umbrellas and walking down a narrow flooded street in Bangkok

blocks.text: All 50 of Bangkok's districts have been declared emergency zones.
Chadchart Sittipunt, the city's governor, said the east of the city had been hardest hit, AFP reported.

He continued: "The rain keeps falling and we are doing our best. We are trying to pump the water out, but the water in canals are full... The risk areas are those who live near canals. Every canal is now filled."

articles.title: White House bars CNN from travelling with Trump on Air Force One
articles.summary: CNN was scheduled to fly with US President Donald Trump for his trip to Tennessee on Saturday.

blocks.text: US broadcaster CNN has been barred from travelling with President Donald Trump on Air Force One for a trip to Tennessee on Saturday.
The move is the latest in a battle between the White House and the media after it was forced to lift its ban on some news outlets.

CNN was scheduled to fly with Trump for his trip to Tennessee for a college American football game until a note released on Friday night by the White House did not list the broadcaster on the media schedule.
The BBC has requested comment from the White House.
CNN has reported that no other outlet was listed as replacing them in the president's tentative schedule.
Last week Trump banned CNN, Politico and MS NOW journalists from the White House after accusing them of writing "fiction or lies" about his administration.
All three media outlets said they were pursuing legal action, and accused Trump of violating their constitutional rights to free speech and freedom of the press.

Four television networks that have a daily rotation of White House coverage along with CNN - ABC, CBS, Fox News and NBC - had paused their broadcasts of the president in solidarity with the banned outlets.
The White House then launched its own streaming channel, Trump TV, ahead of the United General Assembly in New York.
A federal judge has since ruled Trump barring news outlets from the White House was likely unconstitutional and the administration had to let them back in, at least for now.
However, the White House still denied entry to some CNN and MS NOW reporters assigned to cover arrivals for a state dinner for Chinese leader Xi Jinping on Thursday.

A White House communications account earlier posted on X that "contrary to what the Fake News wants you to believe, they don't just get to have free rein into every part of the White House, every event, and every press call".
Regular US television coverage resumed on Friday after White House officials allowed reporters entry.
The president is set to attend a football game between University of Tennessee vs University of Texas College at Neyland Stadium in Knoxville from midday on Saturday.

articles.title: Drones could speed up getting defibrillators to people having cardiac arrests, study suggests
articles.summary:
New research suggests the technology could be used to increase out-of-hospital access to life-saving devices

Drones could help cut the time it takes to get a defibrillator to people…

blocks.text: Drones could help cut the time it takes to get a defibrillator to people experiencing cardiac arrests when not in hospital, researchers have suggested.

In the UK alone, there are more than 30,000 out-of-hospital cardiac arrests a year where emergency medical services attempt to resuscitate the individual, according to the British Heart Foundation. However, fewer than one in 10 people survive such an event, and some who do are left with neurological problems.
One important factor that can affect survival is how rapidly victims get access to treatment – every minute without CPR and defibrillation reduces the chance of survival by 10%.

“We have an objective as EMS [emergency medical service] organisations and EMS physicians to help cardiac arrest patients get defibrillated as early as possible,” said Matthieu Heidet, a professor of emergency medicine at Henri-Mondor university hospital in Créteil, France.
Work by Heidet and colleagues has suggested drones could be used to increase access to the life-saving devices.

To explore the issue, the team analysed the number and location of 28,349 out-of-hospital cardiac arrests that occurred between 2011 and 2024 in administrative areas within the Greater Paris area. Central Paris was excluded from the analysis.
The team cross-referenced these events with the location of fixed automated external defibrillators (AEDs).
The researchers found accessibility of the 1,893 AEDs varied considerably across the area.

“Only 30% of all [out-of-hospital cardiac arrest] cases occurred within the target 500-metre network distance of the nearest recorded fixed AED,” said Dr Hillary Minka, an emergency physician at the Lariboisière hospital in Paris and the first author of the work.

The team found an extra 910 fixed AEDs would be needed for 84.5% of the recorded cardiac arrest cases to have been within 500 metres of an AED, while 1,712 extra fixed AEDs would be needed for 100% coverage.
However, by using drones operating within a radius of 3,900 metres, coverage could be increased with fewer devices.

“As drone bases were introduced, the number of additional fixed AEDs required fell substantially,” said Minka, noting that with 100 drone bases and 26 additional fixed AEDs, more than 97% of the cardiac arrest cases would have been located either within 500 metres of a fixed AED or within approximately 4km (2.5 miles) of a drone base. The use of 200 drone bases and just four extra AEDs meant more than 99% of cases would have been covered.
The researchers also looked at the proportion of the cardiac arrest cases deemed close enough to an existing fixed AED that the device could be retrieved in a round trip within five minutes.
The results revealed only 30-40% of the cardiac arrest cases had access to current fixed AEDs within this time period using the ground transportation network.

Heidet added that this figure was optimistic. “In France, only 8% of out-of-hospital cardiac arrest patients benefit from the application of a public AED before the arrival of the [emergency services],” he said, noting one factor is that a large proportion of AEDs are inaccessible, for example because they are housed in enclosed private spaces that are not open at all times.
after newsletter promotion

By contrast, Minka noted that in a scenario involving 200 drone bases, 871 existing fixed AED sites and four additional fixed AED sites, drone delivery reached virtually all of the cardiac arrest cases covered by the model within five minutes.

The team’s models were based on drones being housed at sites ranging from current AED locations to fire stations and mobile intensive care units, and did not look at real-world deployment of such tech.
Heidet noted it is not the first time drones have been considered for the delivery of AEDs; the approach is already being used in parts of Sweden and has saved lives.
In real-world systems, Heidet added, drones are operated by trained drone pilots.

“Once an emergency call is received and an [out-of-hospital cardiac arrest] is identified at the dispatch centre, the drone is activated by EMS dispatchers. It then takes off and follows an automated flight path, while the final approach and subsequent AED delivery are handled by the drone pilot. The entire process is conducted under the supervision of the emergency medical service,” he said. Once delivered, the AED can be used by members of the public at the scene.
Heidet added the cost of drones needed to be integrated into the evaluation of such technology, noting there may be a balance between the ideal model and the feasible economic model.
The study, which has not yet been peer-reviewed, is to be presented at the European Emergency Medicine Congress in Paris on Saturday.

articles.title: Brazil's Lula bans online gambling ahead of presidential election
articles.summary: Lula, who is currently in a tight presidential race against Flávio Bolsonaro, said the industry was a "cancer" that he must "remove".

blocks.text: Brazilian President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva has announced a ban on online gambling, just days before an election in which he is seeking a fourth term as the country's leader.
Lula, who is running against the son of the incarcerated former Brazilian President Jair Bolsonaro, signed a provisional order on Friday that "prohibits all sports betting and online casinos".
The online gambling industry in Brazil was legalised in 2018 and has since been blamed for widespread household income losses due to addiction.
Lula described the industry as a "cancer" in his announcement, adding "either we remove the tumour, or it kills us".
The move comes just over a week before the first round of voting in Brazil's presidential election. Recent polls have the 80-year-old leader almost neck-and-neck with Flávio Bolsonaro.
The new measures must receive congressional approval within 120 days to remain in force.
Lula acknowledged online betting was created under the former President Michel Temer's administration but that it "grew without regulation under Bolsonaro's management", in a statement on X .
He said that there were "no restrictions" particularly for preventing children and adolescents from accessing online betting.
"We won't allow betting companies to profit at the expense of Brazilian families' income and lives," the president added.
The president described how he had heard from families who had sold everything in their houses because of their gambling addictions.
Separate to the online betting order, Lula also signed a bill to penalise criminal offences related to fixed-odds betting.
Earlier this week, at the United Nations General Assembly, Lula accused the industry of "transforming addiction into profit".
But Flávio Bolsonaro called the gambling crackdown "populist, hypocritical and politically motivated" during a campaign rally in Rio de Janeiro on Friday, according to Reuters.
Most types of gambling, such as casinos and slot machines, are illegal in Brazil, but ever since online betting was legalised in 2018, it has exploded in popularity.
About 59.9% of Brazilian adults support banning internet betting, a survey by Atlas and Bloomberg published this week has found.

articles.title: British climber, 28, dies in fall in northern Spain
articles.summary:
Mountaineer’s body recovered about 20 metres below the summit of Torrecerredo, the highest peak of the Picos de Europa range

A British man has died after falling about 61 metres (200ft)…

blocks.text: A British man has died after falling about 61 metres (200ft) while descending from the summit of a mountain in northern Spain, according to local law enforcement.

The 28-year-old mountaineer fell down a vertical gully on the east side of the Torrecerredo – the highest peak of the Cantabrian mountains – on Thursday afternoon, the Spanish Civil Guard for the Asturias region said.
The mountaineer’s remains were located after a rescue team aboard a helicopter flew over the area, the Civil Guard said.
Two specialists were lowered to retrieve the man’s body and his belongings which had been scattered during the fall.
The incident occurred during the descent, about 20 metres below the Torrecerredo peak, the Civil Guard said.
The mountaineer’s body was transported to La Morgal, a regional sports and aviation facility in Llanera near the Asturian city of Gijon.
A spokesperson for the UK Foreign Office said it had contacted local authorities about the death.
Torrecerredo, which has an elevation of about 2,649 metres, is the highest peak of the Picos de Europa mountain range, which is part of the larger Cantabrian Mountains range.

articles.title: South African white genocide does not exist, new ambassador to US tells BBC
articles.summary: Roelf Meyer tells the BBC that being a white Afrikaner gives him legitimacy to challenge Trump's claim of a genocide.
articles.byline: Ione Wells, Mayeni Jones, Ed Habershon

blocks.text: South Africa's new ambassador to Washington has a personal reason to challenge Donald Trump's assertion that there is a genocide against white Afrikaners - he is "a born Afrikaner" himself.
"Is he talking about us?", Roelf Meyer remembers thinking, when he first heard President Trump say it.
His response to the US president's claim is blunt.
The notion of a mass attack on the white Afrikaner minority in South Africa does not exist, he told the BBC, adding that his identity gave him the legitimacy to say so.

Meyer was one of the chief mediators to end white-minority rule known as apartheid in South Africa in the 1990s. He was appointed ambassador to the US in April, after diplomatic relations between the US and South Africa plummeted.

In an interview with the BBC, Meyer said the facts about violence in South Africa had been misrepresented and he never got a clear answer about where this "misdirection of information" was coming from.
Last year, Trump accused South Africa of white genocide in a meeting with President Cyril Ramaphosa at the White House and launched a US refugee pathway for Afrikaners.
Since last year, nearly 13,000 refugees were admitted to the United States and all but three were South African.
Among them was Lielie, the name she uses publicly, who moved with her family to Texas from South Africa, where they had lived on her stepfather's farm, growing macadamia nuts and bananas.
Despite walls around the house, an electric fence, and eight bull terriers, she said she felt "fear the whole time" and that on three occasions she saw people entering her property.
"Nothing was stolen, we weren't harmed, but there are friends of my husband, people that lived around us, they were brutally attacked," she said.
She said since moving to the US under the Trump administration's refugee pathway her life had changed, she felt safer walking around, and "my kids can actually play outside".
The Trump administration is planning to admit up to 17,500 additional white Afrikaners as refugees over the next 12 months, according to a notice sent to Congress on Tuesday.

In a statement to the BBC, a White House spokeswoman said: "President Trump has provided a lifeline for Afrikaners, who are being raped, maimed, killed and driven off their property across South Africa.

"While the South African government and many in the media have brushed off the horrific lived experiences of this community, the Trump administration continues to process applications for refugee status because the president has a humanitarian heart."
SJ Du Venage, who lives on South Africa's west coast, has been trying to move to the US under the new scheme.
Du Venage is a council member of the Freedom Front Plus, a right-wing Afrikaner party, and argues that there is a "political drive towards killing white people, and killing the farmers on the farms".
"There's absolutely an agenda to wipe us out here," he says.
An Afrikaner lobby group is holding a vigil on Saturday with thousands of white crosses on Washington's National Mall to commemorate what it says are victims of "farm attacks".
Claims of genocide against white South Africans have been discredited by every political party in the country, including by those representing Afrikaners.
"I'm an Afrikaner from South Africa myself," Ambassador Meyer said, "and I can say that I've never experienced something of that kind."
Meyer said he would like to have a conversation with Trump about the reality of the situation, saying that as a "born Afrikaner", he has the "legitimacy" to speak about the subject.

The ambassador helped negotiate an end to apartheid on behalf of the National Party, which was responsible for it, with now-president Cyril Ramaphosa also a key negotiator for the African National Congress party.
He said the "trust" between the two men was one reason President Ramaphosa appointed him to help mend US-South Africa relations, as well as "the fact he also saw the value of me being an Afrikaner".
"But I'm not here to represent the Afrikaner only," Meyer says.

Last week, the Trump administration announced visa restrictions for those South Africans who it said were responsible for "race-based discrimination" against white people. It also warned of further punitive actions if South African leaders did not address the issue.

Police data shows the majority of victims of crime in South Africa, including on farms, are black. Farm violence, often motivated by robberies, is an issue but represents a smaller number of homicides in the country.
While no politician disputes that crime is a problem in South Africa, many experts say this does not qualify as "persecution".

Larry Bartlett, the former director of the US Refugee Assistance Programme, said it could even be "unlawful" to appropriate a programme defined in law for people who "really have no chance to go home".
He said white people who were unlikely to qualify as refugee in law were taking scarce opportunities meant for those fleeing war or ethnic cleansing.

Alongside "rural safety", the Trump administration has raised other concerns about South Africa, including targets for companies to increase non-white employment and a law allowing the state, in exceptional circumstances, to expropriate land without compensation. These are aimed at redressing historic racial inequality.
Meyer wants Trump's executive order against South Africa, which underpins the refugee pathway, revoked.
He said South Africa had never prevented people from leaving and had addressed all the US concerns, stressing that the land expropriation law is awaiting a court judgement.
"South Africa has challenges with the prevention of crime and with the combatting of crime," he said.

But he added: "It's a problem all around. It's not rural. It's not farm attacks only. If you look at the total picture, the huge levels of crime in the black townships of South Africa are the biggest concern, proportionally, far more than anything else."
He said he would encourage the US to help South Africa with resources on combatting crime, including by providing equipment to speed up reaction times.
Meyer also has a message for Afrikaners protesting against "farm attacks" by laying white crosses in Washington.
"It doesn't help us to raise a voice outside, if we are not committed to doing something inside the country," he says.

articles.title: As Merz scrambles for support, Germany's identity crisis is laid bare
articles.summary: Voters are turning away from the centre in Germany as fears grow about the economy and migration.

blocks.text: A set of bumper local elections has thrown Germany, and its government, off balance.
Chancellor Friedrich Merz may now be a man on borrowed time. His coalition government is in crisis.
But this breakdown of business as usual in Germany has been brewing for years.
It's a nation wrestling with new, uncomfortable and unresolved realities.
Think of certain stereotypes about Germany, and think again.
A country dominated by boring, consensus-driven politics? Not any more.
A confident, powerhouse economy at the cutting edge of car-making? Yesterday's story.
A nation that can be used as a byword for impressive efficiency? The trains don't even run on time.
Many Germans I've spoken to feel their nation has drifted away from the things that once anchored their identity.
And the question of what next is, as yet, unanswered.
That uncertainty is currently embodied by a beleaguered chancellor weakened by bruising regional election results.
In the last fortnight, Friedrich Merz's party was beaten to first place in Berlin, pummelled in the polls in Saxony-Anhalt and pushed out of parliament altogether in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania.
A lifeline for Merz is that no-one, within his own centre-right CDU party, is yet willing to challenge the chancellor openly despite persistent rumours of a Kanzlertausch (chancellor swap).
But he is on thin ice, with record low approval ratings among voters who often describe him as arrogant and out of touch.
It is a problem that in government circles is sometimes more politely referred to as a "communication" issue.
Those who back the Chancellor say it is time to double down on much-needed reforms, alongside its centre-left SPD coalition partner, and find a better way of talking to people.
Swapping chancellors is not the answer as anyone would face the "same challenges", argues Jürgen Hardt, foreign policy spokesperson in parliament for Merz's CDU and its sister party, the CSU.

Hardt pointed out that the CDU/CSU fared far better in other regional elections earlier this year, when we spoke minutes after Merz addressed party lawmakers at a closed-door meeting in the Bundestag.

"I think Friedrich Merz knows about his deficits," says Hardt. "He will work on him and we will work on us as (a) party. And hopefully we will convince the people in the next months that we are on the right way."
Merz came to power in 2025, promising to get tough on immigration and boost Germany's ailing economy.
He appeared to offer a dynamism that might act as an antidote to the former dull, unhappy drumbeat of centre-left leader Olaf Scholz's bickering three-way coalition.
And Merz's allies would claim he has had some success.
This week, leading economic institutes raised the country's growth forecasts for 2026 and 2027 above 1% while illegal entries into Germany – and Europe – are down year on year.
But that will not eliminate public anxieties, on either issue.
Households and businesses continue to endure high energy costs while fears persist that China is cannibalising German industry, including its iconic car sector.
It is a brutal reversal of Germany's old recipe for success: cheap Russian gas that powered a booming export-driven economy.
And when it comes to immigration, the focus is now less on new arrivals and more on concerns about public safety, welfare costs and integration.
While there are local exceptions, voters appear to be losing faith in Germany's two principal governing parties (CDU and SPD).

Enter the rising force in German politics, Alternative für Deutschland (AfD): a party that alarms security officials with its Russia-friendly stance and contains regional branches that are classed as right-wing extremist by domestic intelligence.
Smears and misrepresentations, argues the AfD, as it claimed its third victory ever in a state election last Sunday in the north-eastern state of Mecklenburg-West Pomerania.
Its co-leader, Alice Weidel, told me this week that Friedrich Merz's days were numbered.

articles.title: Inside the FBI hack: Agents fearful and angry after 'dangerous' data breach
articles.summary: Current and former agents speak to the BBC about the devastating impact of the FBI hack.

blocks.text: Current and former FBI agents have spoken to BBC News of their shock, fear and anger following a hack that appears to have exposed the private and personal information of the agency's entire workforce.
"This is really bad for our undercover agents," says one former FBI agent, who fears for the safety of his colleagues.
The former cyber investigator is in a group chat with current agents who are worried their personal information could soon be freely available online to criminals and hostile nation-state hackers.
He says staff fear they could be targeted, or that criminals could use the data to create highly convincing phishing attempts, scams or demands for bribes.
The hacking group ShinyHunters is threatening to publish the stolen databases and documents within four days unless its demands are met.
Some agents are also concerned about the risk of physical attacks from cyber criminals they have investigated.
"One of the things we are discussing in the group chat is 'violence-as-a-service' attacks from young online gangs," says the former worker.
"They could use this information to harass an FBI agent who has worked on their cases."

Groups similar to ShinyHunters - believed to be an English-speaking gang - have in the past been linked to swatting incidents, and even petrol bomb attacks against law enforcement officers and rivals.
The group claims it breached FBI systems on Monday and later posted details of the attack on its darknet site.
The FBI has not responded to requests for comment.
However, on Wednesday the agency acknowledged the breach - saying it was "aggressively investigating" how it occurred.

For Michael McPherson, a former FBI agent who is now senior vice president of security operations at cyber firm ReliaQuest, the hack presents "a security threat which cuts to the core of agent safety, particularly their families".
He says agents understand the "inherent risks" that come with the job.

"But this incident reportedly includes personal data such as home addresses and contact information, which could expose family members who are normally insulated from the threats associated with such a career," McPherson says.
ShinyHunters shared samples of the alleged stolen data with reporters, along with an extortion demand.
The samples appear genuine and include names, addresses, phone numbers, badge numbers, job titles and information about spouses.
The records appear to relate to thousands of agents, including senior officials such as deputy directors.
The criminals also appear to possess highly sensitive medical information relating to thousands of special agents.

BBC News has seen samples of stolen "fitness-for-work" medical examinations containing information such as blood and urine test results, along with doctors' notes mentioning conditions including a "shellfish and banana allergy".
Agents' full names and addresses, as well as references to medical issues including "blood in the urine" and "high cholesterol" are now in the criminals' hands.

Cynthia Kaiser, who was the Deputy Director of Cyber at the FBI and now leads the Research Centre at Halcyon says ShinyHunters appear to already have lost control of some of the data which is circulating in various online groups of cyber researchers and could lead to harm even before the main tranche is published.
"A lot of the damage may already be done, and as we have seen in past FBI data breaches, that information continues to circulate the dark web years later," she said.
There are also concerns about the breach's national security implications, such as staff becoming targets for recruitment efforts by hostile foreign intelligence services.
Alongside fear, many of those who spoke to the BBC expressed anger at the FBI for allowing the data to be stolen.
The hack is particularly embarrassing from a technical perspective because ShinyHunters is not generally regarded as a highly sophisticated hacking group.
One former cyber agent said FBI staff were furious about the "sloppy and lazy security failures" that allegedly enabled the breach.
There is also confusion about how to handle any fallout if data is published next week, as threatened.
The FBI appears unlikely to comply with the extortion demands, and the hackers have indicated they intend to post the information on their darknet site.
Unusually, the group is not demanding money. Instead, it wants the FBI to retract an advisory published in May, which it claims "offended" them.
"The agency leadership is lost," the former cyber investigator tells me.
He says staff have been advised to sign up to a service called DeleteMe, which helps remove personal information from data broker websites - a response he feels is inadequate.

articles.title: OpenAI investigating 'dozens' of instances of agents acting improperly
articles.summary: OpenAI agents tried to get information from "governments, universities, public agencies, and other institutions" through extreme means that sometimes curbed security controls, the company said.

blocks.text: OpenAI said Friday it had alerted "dozens" of global institutions that their websites may have been impacted by its AI agents acting improperly.
OpenAI agents attempted to get information from "governments, universities, public agencies, and other institutions" through sometimes extreme means, the company said.

While some of the activity was simply due to the tools working to find "authoritative sources of public information," some went beyond that. Like an AI agent taking and transferring data when it should not have, OpenAI said.
Such activity resulted in at least 53 incidents where an OpenAI agent took an image from ChatGPT user activity and transferred it elsewhere.
The company said that in each instance of a user image being used and transferred by an AI agent, the user had allowed OpenAI to train models using their data.
Nevertheless, OpenAI admitted, "This is not an appropriate use of this data".
It added that the leak of user images occurred before it had put in place new safeguards on AI training, and it was working to get all the user images transferred to any third-party removed.
Reuters first reported these issues.

OpenAI also indicated on Friday that its software may have circumvented certain security controls of the sites impacted - though it doesn't necessarily mean each incident led to a significant security breach.

"Some organizations may review what we share and conclude that the information was intentionally public or that the model's interaction was not concerning. Others may identify a design issue or security weakness they want to address," the company said.

OpenAI said it came across the incidents during an investigation that started after it learned that its AI models had hacked the AI platform Hugging Face, an incident that was revealed publicly last month.

The disclosures on Friday comes just days after Australian's Prime Minister Anthony Albanese said OpenAI had breached non-public files on the website of its government-run health care scheme, Medicare.

articles.title: Michigan CEO loses job after posting AI-made image of her family in ‘Lake America’ sweaters
articles.summary:
Jane Smith reportedly used ChatGPT to edit photo to show name Trump ordered US agencies to use for Lake Ontario amid trade war with Canada

The CEO of a

blocks.text: The CEO of a Michigan credit union is no longer employed there, according to the organization, after she posted on social media what appeared to be an AI-generated image of her and her family wearing sweaters emblazoned with the Donald Trump-associated words “Lake America”.
In the statement recently announcing that Jane Smith would no longer be its CEO, Family First Credit Union also apologized “for the concern, disappointment and pain this situation has caused”.

Smith had been the chief executive officer of the Family First Credit Union when she posed for a family photo at the Detroit airport en route to Halifax, Canada. She reportedly used ChatGPT to edit the family’s sweaters to say Lake America, which since late August has been the name that Trump ordered the US’s federal government agencies to use for Lake Ontario amid the president’s trade war with Canada.
Smith then shared the image on Facebook on 11 September – the 25th anniversary of the 9/11 terrorist attacks in the US – along with the caption: “Like our sweatshirts? Not sure Canada will.”
The post ended with “Lol lol”. It went viral and then provoked backlash from people in Canada – where a portion of the lake is.
Those online users found it disrespectful, and the post has since been deleted according to Canadian Broadcasting Corporation (CBC) News.

Many in the comments highlighted that the post was particularly insensitive, given Halifax’s role in hosting thousands of stranded airplane passengers who were diverted there when US airspace closed on the day of the 9/11 attacks.

As the controversy intensified, Family First Credit Union – based in Saginaw, Michigan – said it was reviewing the situation. Smith, meanwhile, apologized, expressing regret, maintaining that the post was the result of poor judgment and saying that she understood why it would be offensive.

“We weren’t trying to make a political statement,” Smith told the Detroit television news station WJRT. “However, we were, you know, kind of poking fun” at the changing of the name of one of the Great Lakes.

“I understand if I was someone in Halifax and I thought a poor group of people walked in wearing those sweatshirts, it is highly offensive and I would understand why they would be so angry,” she continued in her remarks to WJRT. “I am not a person that would ever want to offend or hurt anybody.
“I do regret having any post that would make someone feel like we don’t value them as human beings.”
Despite her apology, the credit union made it clear that it had parted ways with Smith.
“Jane Smith is no longer employed by Family First Credit Union, effective immediately,” said a statement from the organization shared on social media.

After saying Smith’s interim successor would be Jason Acosta, the statement continued, “We sincerely apologize for the concern, disappointment and pain this situation has caused our members and community.

“We understand that members of our community may hold different perspectives about this decision. Our responsibility is to act in the best interest of the Credit Union, uphold the trust of our members and continue putting our community first.”
Family First Credit Union’s statement about Smith came after broader repudiation in Canada and beyond of Trump’s executive order changing Lake Ontario’s name to Lake America.

Canada’s prime minister, Mark Carney, explained in a post on social media that the body of water’s name comes from the language of the Indigenous Wendat people – and predates both the Canadian Confederation and the US’s declaration of independence from the UK.
“Canadians … know that naming reality means calling it Lake Ontario – then, now and always,” he wrote on X.
Several US governors in the US’s Great Lakes region also dismissed the name change. Michigan borders the Canadian province of Ontario along with four of the five Great Lakes.
The only one of the Great Lakes that Michigan does not border is Lake Ontario. New York is the only US state that Lake Ontario borders.

Trump’s order has no authority to rename Canada’s portion of the lake. It also has no power to compel Canada, international legal bodies, international mapmakers or the rest of the world to adopt a new name.

articles.title: The treasured 'eternal snow' on this tropical island is about to disappear forever
articles.summary: Climate change is transforming Papua's snowy peaks, which hold scientific value and spiritual significance.

blocks.text: The treasured 'eternal snow' on this tropical island is about to disappear forever
Image source, Project Pressure/Klaus Tymann
Only small patches of snow remain on Papua's Sudirman Range
ByAbraham Utama
BBC Indonesia
The mountains of Papua are not far from the equator, but they've been topped with "eternal snow" for centuries.
The peaks in this Indonesian region on the world's second-largest island, just north of Australia, have offered scientists countless insights into the Earth's climate history.
They're also the epicentre of the spiritual universe for many Papuans - a Mecca or a Vatican, as one activist puts it.
But now, nearly all the snow is gone.
A century ago, the 300km (190-mile) stretch of the Sudirman Range had snow and permanent ice on all four of its major peaks.
But now there are only small areas around Puncak Jaya, also known as Carstensz Pyramid, with any snow at all. These are expected to entirely disappear in a year or two.

Glacier cover around the peak has shrunk from nearly 1,900 hectares (4,700 acres) in the 19th Century to about 16 hectares (40 acres) today. Almost entire glaciers have vanished within a human lifetime.

blocks.caption: Map and satellite image showing rapidly shrinking glaciers around Puncak Jaya in Indonesia's Papua region. Labels mark nearby peaks including Sumantri, Ngga Pulu and Carstensz East, with a callout noting that glaciers near the peaks are disappearing. An inset map locates Papua on the island of Ne…

blocks.text: "There is a profound unfairness in this," says Marie Šabacká, a Czech glacier ecologist who travelled to Puncak Jaya last March in a bid to be among the last scientists to study Papua's "eternal snow".

She says the tropical glaciers in Papua are unique because they are separated from other glacier systems by thousands of kilometres. Papua is home to the "last remaining tropical ice" between the Andes and Himalayas.
Ice cores taken from the slopes of Puncak Jaya preserve a record of climate history.

Scientists can use them to obtain information about atmospheric conditions in the region and understand changes in the planet's warmest ocean waters that surround the island - the tropical Pacific and Western Pacific Warm pool.
But this archive is disappearing before scientists have had time to fully study it.

blocks.caption: Image caption, The snow cover has reduced dramatically since this photo, taken in 1936

blocks.text: The snow cover has reduced dramatically since this photo, taken in 1936
Proof of a warming planet

The retreat of Papua's glaciers is driven by the same forces affecting ice around the world, Šabacká notes, a warming atmosphere caused by human activity, including the burning of fossil fuels like coal, oil and gas.
